The natural coefficient map sends each integral generator \(u^k\) to the nonzero generator of the corresponding rational group. Thus the rational ring is \(\mathbb Q[u_{\mathbb Q}]\), with \(|u_{\mathbb Q}|=2\). [A1, F4, F5]

contract_changes.after: Let \(\chi:T\to S^1\) be a smooth character and restrict it to each coordinate one-parameter subgroup \(\gamma_i(s)=[0,\ldots,s,\ldots,0]\). Write \(f_i(s)=\chi(\gamma_i(s))\). The homomorphism law gives \(f_i(s+h)=f_i(s)f_i(h)\); differentiating in \(h\) at zero yields \(f_i'(s)=f_i(s)f_i'(0)\). Since \(|f_i(s)|=1\), differentiation of \(|f_i(s)|^2=1\) at zero shows \(f_i'(0)=2\pi i a_i\) for a real \(a_i\). By [F9], the derivative of \(e^{-2\pi i a_i s}f_i(s)\) is zero, so [F10] makes it constant \(1\); hence \(f_i(s)=e^{2\pi i a_i s}\). Since \(\gamma_i(1)\) is the identity, \(f_i(1)=1\) and [F9] gives \(a_i=n_i\in\mathbb Z\). The product decomposition of \(T\) now gives \(\chi([t])=e^{2\pi i\sum_i n_i t_i}\). Uniqueness follows by restricting again to each \(\gamma_i\). [F9, F10, given, construct]

contract_changes.before: For \(k=\mathbb Q\) or \(\mathbb R\), [F6] applied to the same integral chain complex and \(G=k\) gives \(H_n(\mathbb{CP}^{\infty};k)=k\) for even \(n\) and zero for odd \(n\), since the integral groups in [F4] are free. Iterating [F11] over the finite product in step 1.2 identifies \(H_n(BT;k)\) with a direct sum over the finitely many \(r\)-tuples of nonnegative degrees summing to \(n\). Every summand is either zero or one-dimensional over \(k\), so \(H_n(BT;k)\) is finite-dimensional, and therefore finite-free, for every \(n\). For \(r=0\), only the degree-zero group \(k\) occurs. [A1, F4, F6, F11, step 1.2, algebra]
